Nourished
NUR-isht
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Old French norir, from Latin nutrire, to suckle, to feed, to bring up. Webster 1828: fed; supported; brought up; nurtured. The word carries the sense of long feeding rather than a single meal, which is exactly why Paul chooses it for a minister’s formation.

Biblical Definition

Paul’s picture of a faithful minister is not a man with a gift but a man who has been fed: thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained (1 Timothy 4:6). The tense and the compound both point backward — Timothy is what years of doctrine have made him, and the immediately preceding clause tells him how to keep it up: by putting the brethren in remembrance of these things. A man is nourished by the doctrine he feeds to others. Luke uses the same word for an infancy that shaped a deliverer: Moses, when he was cast out, Pharaoh's daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son (Acts 7:21). James turns it into an indictment, and the image is agricultural and terrible: Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter (James 5:5) — men fattening themselves on the very day the beasts are killed. The word can even describe a dependency between nations: Tyre and Sidon sought peace with Herod because their country was nourished by the king's country (Acts 12:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NOURISH as to feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste of its organs; to support; to maintain; to educate; hence NOURISHED, fed, supported, brought up.

expand to see more

NOURISH, v.t. — To feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste of its organs.

To support; to maintain by feeding; as, to nourish a family.

To educate; to instruct; to bring up; to promote growth in attainments.

To cherish; to encourage; to foster; as, to nourish a hope, or a rebellion.

NOURISHED, pp. — Fed; supplied with nutriment; caused to grow; educated. Latin nutrio, to feed.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 4:6 — "If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained."

Acts 7:21 — "And when he was cast out, Pharaoh's daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son."

James 5:5 — "Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter."

Acts 12:20 — "And Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon: but they came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus the king's chamberlain their friend, desired peace; because their country was nourished by the king's country."

Modern Corruption

1 Timothy 4:6 makes doctrine the minister’s food rather than his equipment, which the modern pastorate has largely inverted by treating theology as a seminary stage to be passed.

expand to see more

Paul does not tell Timothy to use good doctrine; he says a good minister is nourished up in it, and the metaphor is nutrition, not tooling. Doctrine is what a man is made of, laid down over years, and the loss of that picture is the root of much that ails the modern pastorate. Where theology is treated as a credential obtained early and thereafter drawn upon, a ministry runs on stored reserves and eventually on technique. Where it is treated as daily food, it keeps building the man. Notice too the order of the verse: Timothy is nourished by putting the brethren in remembrance — the feeding of the flock is part of how the shepherd is fed. The Puritan practice of preaching one’s way through Scripture, and the confessional practice of catechizing, both assume this and are worth recovering for this reason alone.

James 5:5 supplies the counter-image and it is the sharper of the two: ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter. The rich men James addresses are feeding themselves well, and the figure is livestock fattened on the very morning the knife is out. Scripture’s objection is not to wealth as such — Abraham and Job were rich, and Scripture does not apologize for it — but to a heart nourished by pleasure and indifferent to the judgment standing at the door (James 5:9). It is worth naming the prosperity teaching here in the same breath: a gospel that promises exactly the fattening James condemns, and calls the fattening evidence of God’s favour, has read this chapter backwards.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek entrepho (G1789), to nourish up in, to train; anatrepho (G397), to bring up, to rear; trepho (G5142), to feed or fatten.

expand to see more

Greek entrepho (G1789) — to nourish up in, to train within something; nourished up in the words of faith (1 Timothy 4:6).

Greek anatrepho (G397) — to bring up, to rear from infancy; used of Moses in Pharaoh’s house (Acts 7:21).

Greek trepho (G5142) — to feed, and of animals to fatten; ye have nourished your hearts (James 5:5).

Greek sphage (G4967) — slaughter; the day on which James’s rich men are fattening (James 5:5).

Greek didaskalia (G1319) — teaching, doctrine; the substance Timothy is nourished in (1 Timothy 4:6).

Usage

"Nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine (1 Timothy 4:6) — doctrine as food, not as equipment."

"Nourished him for her own son (Acts 7:21) — providence rearing a deliverer in the house of the oppressor."

"Ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter (James 5:5) — livestock fattened on the morning the knife is out."
